extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, applicants, and IP office / IP policy staff in ASEAN Member States
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and best-practice standards for examination, opposition, appeals, expedited procedures, and patentable subject-matter applicable across ASEAN Member States (AMS). Intended to guide examiners, applicants and third parties on procedural and substantive requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-sharing / PPH / Recognition programmes
rubrics_metrics.description: AMS have entered into bilateral PPH programmes and “Recognition”/“Validation” agreements with other patent offices; these can be paired with ASPEC programmes to expedite examination and grant of patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These programmes facilitate expedited examination by relying on outcomes or work from other offices. See Chapter 14 for more details on bilateral PPHs and recognition/validation agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: National fast-track / expedited examination programmes (Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore)
rubrics_metrics.description: Malaysia, Thailand and Singapore provide domestic fast track programmes for expediting examination and grant of patents with specific caps, technical-field restrictions, and conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common conditions include: applicant must indicate reason for expedited examination; caps on number of applications per month and per entity; field restrictions (e.g., medical/public health in Thailand pilot); limits on number of claims (e.g., Thailand: 10 claims); deadlines for responding to adverse S&E reports (e.g., 3 weeks in Malaysia/Thailand). Expected grant timetables (e.g., Singapore: less than 12 months from filing; Thailand: up to 12 months for invention patent and 6 months for petty patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of patentable subject matter during substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner assesses patentability of subject matter during substantive examination (exception: Viet Nam assesses in both formalities and substantive examination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because assessing patentable subject matter is usually complex, it is recommended that such assessment be conducted during substantive examination by examiners well versed in patentability conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of substantive examination reports to third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive examination report should be made available to third parties at the latest after the granting date of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication of substantive examination reports enhances transparency and assists third parties in opposition or post-grant activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant right to respond to substantive examination objections
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent office issues an objection, the applicant must be allowed to file a response (e.g., explanation, data, or evidence) suitable for addressing the objections raised by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the response will be admitted depends on the individual case. If the examiner upholds the rejection, the applicant may appeal to an upper administrative body or competent court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and procedure for appeal of substantive examination report
rubrics_metrics.description: Following receipt of the substantive examination report, the applicant may file an appeal against a decision rejecting a patent based on an unresolved objection through administrative and judicial procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal should be available as part of remedies against rejection; procedures vary by AMS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum content of a substantive examination report
rubrics_metrics.description: The minimum information in a substantive examination report should include: assessment of patentability; search report (if applicable); list and details of cited prior arts including patent and non-patent literature; grounds for rejecting the application and explanation; deadline to respond to an objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language is normally the official language of the filing country; some AMS (Brunei, Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore) generally produce examination reports in English. Substantive reports should be sufficiently detailed to permit meaningful response and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and nature of pre-grant and post-grant opposition actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition actions provide third parties an opportunity to oppose the grant of a patent on at least one ground (e.g., lack of novelty). They are inter partes proceedings (generally before the patent office) designed to ensure quality and validity of granted patents by early rectification of invalid patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oppositions may be pre-grant (after publication of application) or post-grant (after grant). They are typically inter partes proceedings, not courts, and aim to be simple, fast, and inexpensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-grant opposition procedural features
rubrics_metrics.description: In some AMS, a person may submit an opposition or objection form within prescribed time periods after publication; the opponent must state grounds and submit evidence and pay fees; applicant is notified and may respond within prescribed time limit; examiner decides based on submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some countries (Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore) any person may present written observations on patentability which the examiner should consider. Pre-grant opposition often begins after positive formality examination and publication of claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant opposition procedural features
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AMS (Indonesia, Malaysia) allow post-grant opposition; Singapore allows revocation applications or re-examination. Opposition deadlines start once the patent is granted; opponent files evidence within prescribed time and patentee is notified and may respond; examiner decides whether to maintain, amend, or revoke the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-grant opposition affects only opposed patents (less systemic delay than pre-grant) but creates uncertainty about enforceability during the opposition period and may affect licensing value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-practice features for effective opposition systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-exhaustive enabling factors include: prompt and easy access to full patent applications/granted patents; access to prior art information; reasonable opposition timeframes; reasonable formalities/procedures (inter partes written/oral proceedings; clear rules for supporting evidence and arguments); grounds for opposition that balance quality and legal certainty; rules on interrelationship with invalidation; opportunities for counterclaims and appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing timely resolution and legal certainty is key. Publication of full content of applications/granted patents is a best practice to allow meaningful opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-grant and post-grant oppositions may be filed on grounds that: (1) the claimed invention is not patentable, (2) lacks novelty, (3) lacks inventive step, (4) lacks industrial applicability. Some countries also consider lack of disclosure/support, incorrect amendments, and applicant eligibility as grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds vary by AMS; oppositions must identify grounds and typically include supporting evidence (e.g., prior art documents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties entitled to file opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person/party is allowed to file an opposition action where the law provides an opportunity for opposition (opponents are not universally restricted to 'interested parties').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility to a broad set of potential opponents helps policing patent quality but may increase filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period and right to withdraw an opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The opponent must be able to withdraw its opposition at any time during the proceedings before issuance of the decision by the patent office/registrar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flexibility to withdraw can simplify case management and settle disputes, but timing relative to decisions is restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for patent owner to respond to opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant/patent proprietor must be able to file a counter-statement and/or adduce evidence in response to an opposition filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural fairness requires the patentee to have reasonable opportunity to address allegations before a decision is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal from decisions on opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal against the final decision of the opposition body is generally possible, often before a court; Article 62.5 of TRIPS requires administrative decisions concerning acquisition and maintenance of IP rights to be subject to review by judicial or quasi-judicial authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: in some jurisdictions third party observations are not inter partes (e.g., Malaysia and Philippines) and thus cannot be appealed as oppositions; post-grant invalidation/cancellation decisions may be appealed to the upper court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of foreign patent office decisions in opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition or observation systems should allow consideration of decisions issued by foreign offices on oppositions for the same inventions as part of the arguments in opposition procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign office decisions may be persuasive and relevant evidence but must be evaluated in local legal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party submissions / observations before and during substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: A third-party observation may help identify prior art while examining a patent application; third parties may file observations before and during substantive examination, with or without an obligation to disclose identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party inputs can orient search/examination early; procedures differ by AMS regarding anonymity and admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'invention' for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Invention' means that which is specified in the claim(s) of a patent; in most AMS an invention is defined as a solution to a technical problem that has a technical effect and can be a product, process, or product-by-process. Improvements of known products/processes may also be inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subject matter does not comply with the legal definition of 'invention' or is clearly not an invention, the application will be rejected and other grounds need not be examined. The term 'improvement' does not require superiority over prior art; an alternative providing similar effects may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject-matter / exclusion 'as such'
rubrics_metrics.description: AMS’ patent laws exclude certain subject-matter 'as such' from patentability (non-technical/unpatentable). If a claim comprises excluded subject-matter 'as such' and at least one technical feature then the claimed invention is regarded as statutory subject-matter. One technical feature can be sufficient for eligibility; assessment is made without reference to prior art (exception: Singapore considers technical means but may still exclude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify which features contribute to the technical character. Non-technical features may still contribute to technical character in context if they produce a technical effect serving a technical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: All AMS (except Brunei) explicitly prohibit discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods from patentability because they are abstract and/or lack technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such material is put to practical use producing a technical effect, it may be patentable. Examples: a mere discovery of a material property is unpatentable but a railway sleeper made from that material could be patentable; mathematical methods per se are excluded but a calculating machine implementing them may require search and examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schemes, rules, or methods for doing business; purely mental acts; playing games
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of doing business, purely mental acts, and ways of playing games 'as such' are excluded from patentability because they are abstract and do not produce a technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed subject-matter specifies technical means (e.g., a programmable apparatus) for executing at least some steps, the claim may not be excluded. Examples: pure business methods or game rules claimed in isolation may be excluded; a computer-implemented method with a practical technical application could be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic creations excluded unless technical aspects present
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic creations are excluded from patentability because they lack technical effect, but where an aesthetic creation produces a technical effect or involves technical aspects (e.g., a substrate plus a technical effect), it may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tyre tread pattern providing improved water channeling may be technical and patentable; mere colour of a tyre sidewall serving aesthetic purpose is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of information excluded 'as such'
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation of information (content) is excluded from patentability when directed to the presentation 'as such'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If presentation has technical character or structural/functional relation to the information carrier/process/apparatus (e.g., a gramophone record groove form, a diapositive with a soundtrack), it should be examined. Mere arrangements/compilations of data are generally excluded unless technical character or practical application exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions contrary to public order and morality excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions contrary to public order, morality, peace or security are excluded from patentability to deny protection to inventions likely to induce riot, public disorder, criminal or offensive behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision is for rare/extreme cases; a fair test is whether the public would regard the invention as so abhorrent that granting patent rights would be inconceivable (example: a suicide machine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer programs 'as such' excluded; technical effect required
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer programs (sequences of executable instructions) are abstract and devoid of technical character and are excluded 'as such'. However, inventions implemented by a computer program that produce a 'technical effect' beyond normal physical interactions may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal physical effects (circulation of currents) are insufficient. Examples of technical effects: controlling anti-lock braking, determining emissions, compressing video, restoring distorted images, encrypting communications, security measures protecting boot integrity. Claims must include all technical features essential for the technical effect; product, process and use claims may be allowable where technical character exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step approach for assessing computer program related claims
rubrics_metrics.description: One approach: (1) properly construe the claim; (2) identify the actual contribution made by the invention (examiner not bound by applicant's assertion); (3) determine whether the actual contribution falls solely within excluded subject matter 'as such'; (4) determine whether the contribution is actually technical in nature ('technical contribution').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the contribution has technical character, proceed to examine novelty and inventive step. There is no single fixed AMS-wide criterion; examiners should apply these steps objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented inventions and claim forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A computer-implemented invention covers claims involving computers/networks/programmable apparatus where at least one feature is implemented by a computer program. A computer program and a corresponding computer-implemented method are distinct: the former is a sequence of executable instructions; the latter is a method actually performed on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to a computer-implemented method cannot be objected to on the ground of being non-patentable subject matter because methods involving technical means have technical character; drafting should ensure technical features are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting requirement for computer program claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Because patentability of computer programs depends on technical effect, claims must be drafted to include all technical features essential for the technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where patentability is admitted, product, process and use claims would generally be allowable. The presence of a programmable apparatus or other technical means in the claim may avoid exclusion but is not always determinative (Singapore exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for treatment of the human or animal body excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for treatment of the human or animal body by surgery, therapy, or diagnosis are excluded from patentability to ensure medical practitioners are not hindered by patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therapeutic instruments/apparatus and products/substances for use in therapeutic methods are not excluded. A method claim with even one step defining a therapeutic activity (e.g., administering a prophylactic substance) may render the claim unpatentable. Cosmetic treatments may be patentable unless they involve surgery/therapy.
